v.why: Stacked layers compound the effective step size so high learning rates diverge or saturate more often at greater depth.
With few updates from large batches, a deeper net moves further in function space per Adam step and fits faster.
Strong L2 shrinks every layer and the shrinkage multiplies across layers, pushing outputs toward constant.
Narrow single-layer nets are capacity-limited, so an extra layer adds useful representational power that wide nets already have.
Low-LR runs are step-starved and smaller batches give many more updates within 243 epochs.
A noisier gradient combined with a large Adam step makes updates erratic and can derail training.
Large batches give few updates, so a larger learning rate compensates for the step deficit.
Narrow nets need larger learning rates to fit within 243 epochs and are less prone to divergence.
Wider layers increase the output change per step, so high learning rates become unstable.
Narrow nets are capacity-limited, so extra shrinkage causes underfitting with no overfitting to offset it.

From the remaining 15, I kept 10 with distinct mechanisms. Each pairs an edit with a different condition field, except two batch_size-down hypotheses with learning_rate_init conditions. Those two differ in mechanism (step starvation at low learning rate versus gradient noise at high learning rate). I favored interactions where an expert could reasonably bet either way.
